title: Per-request latency-sensitive pricing — rough notes
content:
Context / goal:
Quick working notes on a pricing axis that prices for latency-sensitive requests at a premium while keeping a PAYG path for less-sensitive workloads. Trying to capture unit-econ math + product tradeoffs. Not polished — notes to self and a couple of numbers to test with finance.

Background assumptions (high level):
- Two usage dimensions matter a lot to customers and to backend cost: tokens (compute work) and latency/priority (scheduling cost & capacity reservation).
- Low-latency requests (e.g., <100ms generation end-to-end for short prompts) force small-batch, reserved capacity and higher unit cost.
- Throughput-oriented workloads (embeddings, async generation, high-TPS requests) can be batched heavily, much lower marginal cost per token.

Key primitives for a pricing design:
1) Per-token base charge (PAYG) — covers average compute amortized across our fleet; encourages efficient prompts.
2) Latency premium multiplier or per-request priority fee — captures the cost of reserving QPS / reducing batching.
3) Reserved QPS / instant credits subscription — for customers who need guaranteed latency, sell capacity blocks (like 1 reserved QPS for X/month) that reduce per-token latency premium.
4) Burst credits — time-limited pool that can be consumed for short high-priority windows.

Core unit-econ sandbox (very rough):
Assumptions:
- Avg cost to Redwood per 1M tokens in mixed workload (after batching/kernels): $6 (hosted average).
- For low-latency path (dedicated or reserved QPS), cost increases 3x because batching opportunities lost, padding, and higher instance footprint -> $18 / 1M tokens equivalent.
- Typical short request: 30 tokens generated (response) + 50 tokens input = 80 tokens / request; so 12.5k requests per 1M tokens.
- Small-request overhead (network, scheduling) makes per-request handling nonzero; we should capture it as a fixed per-request cost in pricing. Assume infra overhead equivalent to $2 / 1M tokens for high-priority path.

Compute examples:
A) PAYG baseline: price = cost * markup. If we want 35% gross margin on hosted average: price_per_1M = $6 / (1 - 0.35) = ~$9.23 -> round to $9 / 1M tokens.
B) Low-latency PAYG: raw cost $18 + overhead $2 = $20 / 1M tokens. To target same margin: 20 / (1 - 0.35) = ~$30.77 -> price ~ $31 / 1M tokens.
C) Hybrid (reserved QPS): Customer buys reserved QPS that amortizes some of the 3x penalty. Example: 1 reserved QPS bucket (24/7) = theoretical max tokens/month if saturated: 1 token/sec * 3600*24*30 = 2.59M tokens/month (if 1 token/sec, unrealistic — better think in requests). Reasonable model: 1 reserved QPS ~ supports 12k small requests/minute? hmm.
-- Simpler: think of reserved QPS as capacity credit: 1 reserved QPS reduces latency premium by 60% when used. So instead of $20/1M, reserved customers pay $20 * 0.4 = $8 / 1M + a monthly reservation fee.
-- If reservation fee = $500/month for 1 QPS, and expected consumption = 2M tokens/month, effective per-1M add-on due to reservation = 500 / 2 = $0.25 / 1M tokens. So economics favor reservation for steady traffic.

Per-request fee model (alternative):
- Charge a small flat per-request priority surcharge (e.g., $0.001 per low-latency request) plus a lower per-token rate. This captures fixed overhead better for tiny-response workloads.
- Example: 80 tokens/request, at $9/1M tokens -> token charge = 80 * 9 / 1e6 = $0.00072. Add per-request latency fee $0.0009 gives total $0.00162 per request -> per-1M-token equivalent ~ $20.25 (since 12.5k requests per 1M tokens). This helps capture fixed scheduling cost.

Bucketed tokens vs continuous credits tradeoffs:
- Bucketed tokens (prepaid credits) are simpler UX for customers and give us cashflow. But they encourage hoarding and may complicate latency-tiering if credits are consumed for bursts.
- Continuous credits (like credits that top-up monthly via subscription) map well to reserved QPS. Easier to enforce guaranteed latency only when credits are active.

Pricing sketches (three-tier quick):
- Standard PAYG: $9 / 1M tokens, no latency guarantees, best-effort batching.
- Priority PAYG: $31 / 1M tokens OR Standard + per-request priority surcharge: $0.001 / request + $9 / 1M tokens. Priority PAYG has best-effort low-latency but no SLA.
- Reserved QPS plan: monthly reservation + discounted priority token price. Reservation example: $500/month / QPS + $8 / 1M tokens for priority traffic served on-reservation.

Behavioral considerations (customer impact):
- Small chatbots with short replies: per-request surcharges will be felt; customers might try to move to batching or longer responses to reduce per-request cost — that's ok, it aligns incentives.
- Startups may prefer simplicity: offer a default Standard PAYG and an auto-upgrade path when 95th percentile latency breaches or when monthly spend exceeds X.
- Observability: surface token breakdown and priority charge per request in console to reduce bill shock.

Open questions / next steps:
1) Validate core cost multipliers with infra/serve team: is 3x penalty for low-latency accurate? Get breakdown of GPU minutes, instance sizing, padding, SLO headroom. (Action: Samir to pull SRE perf calc – JIRA: PRIC-87).
2) Model sensitivity: run scenarios (30k, 300k, 3M tokens/month) to show when reservation becomes cheaper than PAYG priority.
3) UX: how to present per-request surcharge without scaring new users? Maybe hide surcharge for first N requests or include in a "priority addon" toggle in Console.
4) Billing implementation: can we represent per-request flags in records to bill differently? Likely yes but need billing infra ticket.
5) Competitive check: what do major LLM APIs do for latency pricing? Quick scan suggests reserved capacity + higher payg for low-latency is common; need exact comps.

Immediate micro-tests to run (data needed):
- Pull 90/95/99 latencies split by request token size and batch size. How many requests are truly latency-sensitive and small?
- Estimate percent of total tokens coming from requests with <200ms service time. That will tell revenue impact.
- Compute backend cost per token for those small/latency-sensitive requests (Samir).

Quick heuristics for communicating to sales/solutions:
- "Low-latency path is a premium service: up to ~3x token price if not using reserved QPS. Recommend reserved QPS for sustained low-latency needs."
- "Offer per-request priority surcharge for sporadic bursts; offer credits bundles for predictable bursts."

To-dos (short):
- [ ] Ask serving-runtime for refined cost multiplier (Samir).
- [ ] Run scenario MR for three customer archetypes (chatbot SMB, document processing mid-market, high-volume embeddings/pipelines) — Priya.
- [ ] Draft simple one-pager for Console UX with priority toggle and visible estimated cost delta.

Random notes / ramblings:
- Might be useful to offer "latency windows" (e.g., business hours reserved QPS cheaper than 24/7). Many customers only need low-latency during peak hours; selling time-limited reservations would be efficient.
- Consider combining with model-variant routing: serve low-latency requests on smaller models tuned for shorter responses and route long high-quality outputs to cheaper async pools. Pricing should reflect model variants too (different base per-token rates).

End of scratch — will tidy after cost numbers from infra.
